params.why: the number the book would print stays small

stem: The graph of $y = {=a}\cdot {=b}^x {=qs} {=qa}$ cuts the $x$-axis at exactly one point. What is the $x$-coordinate of that point?
solution: Move the constant to the right-hand side: ${=a}\cdot {=b}^x = {=-q}$.
The bases are equal, so the exponents are equal: $x = {=k}$. The graph cuts the $x$-axis at $({=k}, 0)$.
notes: The book's method for an intercept: put y = 0 (x-axis) and solve, here by writing both sides as powers of the same base, as in the book's exponential equations. q = -a*c with c = b^k, so a and q always have opposite signs and the graph really cuts the x-axis exactly once (an exponential graph with a and q of the same sign never reaches the axis, so that case is never drawn). The stem says 'exactly one point' only because that is true by construction. When k = 1 the step 'write b as a power of b' is trivial but true (b = b^1). Every valid instance was substituted back into the equation: y is 0 at the stated x.
